_notes: Dominican career, second pool: the first fifteen years. Preaching, the studium, campus and school, the lay chapter, the bishop's parish, Rome. E3 §11, §14.

events.title: The Priory Church on Sunday
events.body: The priory church has a Sunday congregation of its own, people who drive past three parishes for the preaching, and the prior has put you on the eleven o'clock rota in your first month. {@old_friar} preached it for twenty years. The people in the front rows have opinions about the homily the way people elsewhere have opinions about the weather, and they say them at the door, and the first one says, kindly, that it was very interesting, which in this church is not praise.

choices.label: Spend the week on the next one as if it were a thesis
choices.outcome: It is better and it is a lecture, and the woman at the door says so, and the third Sunday you throw the lecture away on Saturday night and preach one thing, and she says nothing at the door and comes back, which is the praise.

choices.label: Ask the old friar to sit in the back and tell you afterward
choices.outcome: He tells you: too long, too many points, and one good minute in the middle that you did not know was there. He sits in the back for a year. It is the best formation you have had and it was free.

choices.label: Preach your own way and let the front rows come around
choices.outcome: Some of them do, over a year. Some go to the nine o'clock, which the prior notices, and the ones who stay are the ones who wanted the new thing, and the church is a little different for it, and so is the front row.

events.title: The Letter to the Editor
events.body: A columnist in the city paper has written that the Church's teaching on a hard question is a relic and that no educated priest believes it, and named the order as the place where the educated priests are. {@prior} has left the paper on your chair with the column folded out. Nobody has asked you to answer it. The order's motto is on the wall of the refectory, and the columnist has, in a way, asked what it means.

choices.label: Write the letter: what the teaching is, and why an educated priest holds it
choices.outcome: The paper prints it, cut by a third. The columnist replies. The bishop's office sends a note that could be thanks. The house divides over whether it was wise, and the prior, who left the paper on the chair, says nothing either way, which was his answer too.

choices.label: Write something longer and slower, for the order's own review
choices.outcome: It is read by four hundred people, all of whom agreed with you before they started, and the columnist never sees it. It is, however, right, and the regent reads it, and the studium asks you to give a lecture on it, which is a door.

choices.label: Preach on it instead, Sunday, to the people who came
choices.outcome: The homily is the answer the letter would have been and it is heard by three hundred rather than read by thirty thousand, and two of the three hundred write to the paper themselves, better than you would have, and the prior smiles at breakfast.

events.title: The Campus Post
events.body: The order's campus ministry at the state university needs a second chaplain and the provincial has written to the prior rather than to you, since it is the prior's man he is taking. The prior has shown you the letter. Two hundred students at the Sunday Mass, a Thursday night that runs late, and a chaplain, {@confrere}, who has done it alone for four years and is thin. The prior says he can spare you or say he cannot, and that he will say whichever you ask.

choices.label: Ask him to spare you
choices.outcome: He spares you. The campus is another life: no bell, no table, a Mass at nine at night and students at the door at eleven, and the friar you came to help is the best friend you make in the order, and the priory, when you come back, is quieter than you remember.

choices.label: Ask him to say he cannot
choices.outcome: He says it. The provincial sends someone else, who is not suited, and the campus goes through a bad two years and the thin chaplain leaves the order, and you do not know whether that was your doing, and you think about it.

choices.label: Offer one year, and a man found for after
choices.outcome: The provincial takes it, since a year is more than he had. The year is hard and the man is found, by you, from the studium, and the campus is the better for both, and the province notices that you found him.

events.title: The Lay Chapter Wants a Friar
events.body: The lay Dominicans who meet in the priory's parlour on the second Tuesday have lost their spiritual assistant, an old friar who died in Lent, and their prioress has asked the prior for you by name, since you gave a talk in Advent that she remembers. It is a chapter of fourteen, mostly women, mostly over sixty, with a rule, a formation program, and opinions about the order that are older than yours.

choices.label: Take them on, second Tuesdays and whatever else it needs
choices.outcome: It needs a great deal else. Funerals, a formation weekend, a dispute about the rule that runs a year. They are the most Dominican people you know and they teach you the order from the outside, and two of them are at every Mass you ever preach in the city.

choices.label: Take them on, once a month and no more
choices.outcome: They understand, and the prioress does not, and the chapter runs itself as it did before and is kind to you at Christmas, and you are a name on their list, which is not nothing.

choices.label: Ask the prior to send someone with more years
choices.outcome: He sends the old friar's contemporary, who is right for them and dies in two years, and the prioress writes to you then, since she remembers the talk, and this time you say yes.

events.title: The Guest Lecture
events.body: The regent has asked you to give a lecture at the studium on the thing you wrote, to the student brothers and whichever of the faculty come, which is the faculty's way of looking at a man. It is an hour on a Wednesday. {@master_of_students} has said, privately, that the student brothers will like it whatever it is and that the two men in the back row will not, whatever it is, and that the lecture is for the two men.

choices.label: Give it for the two men in the back row
choices.outcome: It is dense and exact and the student brothers are lost by the twenty-minute mark, and the two men in the back row ask the questions that were the point, and one of them says, going out, that the studium could use you, which is a sentence the regent hears.

choices.label: Give it for the student brothers
choices.outcome: It is the lecture they remember. Three of them are preachers on your account. The two men in the back row leave at the half hour, and the regent does not ask again for some years, and you find you do not mind.

choices.label: Try for both and know it will be neither
choices.outcome: It is neither. It is a good hour that nobody minds, which at the studium is a kind of verdict, and the master of students says at supper that you were wise, and the regent says nothing, and you are not asked back, and are not not asked back.

events.title: Invitations
events.body: The name has got out. Three pastors in one month have written to the prior for a Lenten series, a parish mission, and a retreat for the diocesan clergy, which is a bishop's idea, and the prior has put the three letters on the table at breakfast and said the house cannot lose you for nine weeks and that you should choose one, or none, and that he will write the other letters himself.

choices.label: The clergy retreat; it is the one that will not come again
choices.outcome: Forty diocesan priests, five days, and a bishop in the front row. It is the hardest preaching you have done and the most watched, and the bishop's office is warmer to the priory for a decade because of it, and two of the priests write to you every Lent for the rest of your life.

choices.label: The mission; it is what the order is for
choices.outcome: A week in a parish that had forgotten missions. The pastor weeps on the last night, as they do, and the province's promoter of preaching, hearing, writes your name in a book he keeps, and it is the book that matters.

choices.label: None; the house comes first this year
choices.outcome: The prior is surprised and then, at Christmas, says it was the right year to say it, since the house has had a hard one. The letters come again next year, fewer, and you take one, and the name is a little smaller than it was and it holds.

events.title: Seen at the Window
events.body: The dispensation is granted and the house knows what it means: you are at the desk when the bell rings and the stall is empty. {@old_friar} has said nothing for a month and now says, in the cloister, that he saw your light at two and your window empty at Lauds, and asks, not unkindly, what it is you are writing that Lauds could not wait for.

choices.label: Tell him: the whole of it, the book and what it is for
choices.outcome: He listens for a long time and says that he wrote one too, once, and that it is in the library, and that nobody has taken it out in thirty years, and that he does not regret it, and that you should go to Lauds anyway, sometimes, and you do.

choices.label: Say the provincial granted it and the matter is the provincial's
choices.outcome: He says the provincial does not live in the house, and walks on, and it is a year before he speaks to you again in the cloister, and when he does it is to say the book was good, since he read it, which he did not have to.

choices.label: Say nothing, and be in the stall at Lauds the next morning
choices.outcome: He nods at you across the choir, once. The book takes longer. The house forgets there was a dispensation and the provincial's office does not, and the next one is easier to ask for, which is not what you expected.

events.title: The Book Is Done
events.body: It is done. Four years, one dispensation, and a manuscript on the desk that the order's press will take, the editor says, if you cut a chapter, and that a university press might take if you cut three and change the title. {@prior} has asked, at supper, whether the house will now have you back, and it was a joke, and the table laughed, and it was not entirely a joke.

choices.label: The order's press, and cut the chapter
choices.outcome: It is out in a year with the order's shield on the spine. It is read by the people who read such things and by more friars than you expected, and the province thinks of you as a man who finished, which is rarer than a man who wrote.

choices.label: The university press, and cut the three
choices.outcome: It is out in two years with a title you did not choose and it is reviewed, twice, and one of the reviews is unkind and correct, and you are, for a while, someone the wider world has heard of, and the house is proud in the way houses are, which is quietly and with jokes.

choices.label: Neither; put it in the drawer and go back to the house
choices.outcome: The prior is startled and then not. The book is in the drawer for eleven years and a student brother finds it and it is published then, with a preface, and reads as if it were written by a man with time, which it was.

events.title: The Bishop Asks for a Pastor
events.body: The bishop has asked the provincial for a friar to take a parish the diocese cannot staff, on the edge of the city, and the provincial has asked the prior, and the prior has asked you, in that order, and all three have said it is your decision, which means it is not, quite. The parish has a school, a debt, and a Mass in a language you do not have, and the priory would lose you to it for six years at least.

choices.label: Take it, and learn the language
choices.outcome: Six years and then nine. You learn the language badly and then well. The parish becomes the order's in everything but the deed, and the priory sends you a friar a year to help and gets back, each year, a friar who knows what a parish is.

choices.label: Take it for three years, with a second friar and the debt on the diocese
choices.outcome: The bishop's office argues about the debt for a month and gives way, since it has no one else, and the three years are five, and the second friar is the making of the place, and the provincial says you negotiated like a procurator.

choices.label: Say the priory is the order's work and the parish is the bishop's
choices.outcome: The provincial accepts it, since he asked. The bishop's office does not forget. The priory keeps you, and the parish closes in four years, and the bishop's successor, who has heard, is a long time warming to the house.

events.title: The Friar They Come To
events.body: It has happened without your arranging it: the Saturday afternoon confessions in the priory church, which used to be a friar and an empty box, are now a line down the side aisle, and the line is for you. {@prior} has noticed, the other confessors have noticed, and one of them has said at recreation, not quite as a joke, that he supposes you give easier penances.

choices.label: Add hours; the line is the work
choices.outcome: Saturday becomes Friday and Saturday. You hear more confessions in a year than most priests hear in ten and you learn the city from inside it, and the line is there for twenty years, and the other confessors, in time, are glad of it, since it is the church's line and not yours.

choices.label: Send the line down the aisle to the other boxes
choices.outcome: Some go and some wait. The other confessors get the ones who go, and are, each in his way, good for them, and the line is shorter and the church is fuller, and the joke at recreation stops.

choices.label: Answer the joke: no, harder ones
choices.outcome: The table laughs, and the friar does not, and it is true, and he knows it is true, which is why he does not laugh, and it is a year before he is easy with you, and then he asks how you do it, and you tell him.

events.title: The Bottle in the Cell
events.body: There is a friar in the house who drinks. Everyone knows it and nobody has said it, since he is old, and kind, and was a good preacher once, and the prior is a young prior who does not know what to do with an old man who was his novice master. This week he missed the Sunday Mass he was to say and you said it, and found the bottle afterward, in his cell, where he had asked you to fetch his breviary.

choices.label: Tell the prior what you found
choices.outcome: The prior is relieved that it is said. He gets the old man help, which the province has, and it half works, which is what such things do, and the old man says to you, a year on, that he knew it was you and is not sorry, and you are not sure which he means.

choices.label: Speak to him yourself, alone
choices.outcome: He weeps, and denies it, and weeps, and it is a bad hour and a good one, and it is not the last hour, and he stops for a while and starts, and you are the one he telephones at two in the morning for a decade, and you answer.

choices.label: Put the bottle back, and say the Masses
choices.outcome: You say his Masses for a year. The house knows and is grateful and ashamed. He dies in the house, of it, with his brothers around him, and the prior says at the funeral that he was a great preacher, which he was, and nobody says the rest, and it is on you.

events.title: The Question at Table
events.body: A visiting professor from the order's house in Rome has said at table, to a silence, that the province's studium teaches Thomas like a catechism and that no one here has read a philosopher born after 1300. The regent is not at table. {@master_of_students} is. The student brothers are looking at their plates. Someone must answer him, since it was said to the house, and the men senior to you are waiting to see if you will.

choices.label: Answer him: which philosophers, and what they got wrong
choices.outcome: It becomes a two-hour argument that the student brothers remember for years and that the visitor, going, says was the best table he has sat at in the province, and the regent, told, is pleased and a little jealous.

choices.label: Agree with him, partly, and say what the studium could do better
choices.outcome: The senior men are not pleased and the visitor is, and the regent hears both accounts, and the studium adds a course two years later that is, in substance, your answer, and does not say so.

choices.label: Look at your plate with the student brothers
choices.outcome: Someone senior answers him, badly. The visitor leaves the next day. The master of students says nothing about it to you and you find you would rather he had.

events.title: The Order's School
events.body: The order runs a high school in the city, or did: the friars on its staff are down to two, the president is a layman, and the board has asked the provincial for a friar who can teach theology to sixteen-year-olds and say the Friday Mass. The provincial has named you, and the prior has passed it on, and the school's president, a good man in a suit, has taken you to lunch and said the boys will eat you alive unless you are funny.

choices.label: Go; it is where the vocations are
choices.outcome: It is where the vocations are. Five boys in ten years ask about the order, and two enter, and one stays, and it is the only thing anyone in the province counts, and you are funny, it turns out, when you have to be.

choices.label: Go, on condition the school gives you a class of your own and not just the Mass
choices.outcome: The board agrees, since it wanted the Mass. The class is the point. Forty boys a year read Thomas on the virtues and some of them understand it, and the president says at a dinner that the school has a theology department again, and means you.

choices.label: Decline; the school is a school and you are a preacher
choices.outcome: The provincial sends someone else, who is eaten alive. The school is a lay school in everything but its name in five years. The province, which has been losing its schools for forty years, does not blame you, and does not forget either.

events.title: The Chant Is Going
events.body: The house's chant is going. The men who could sing are old or moved, the young men have not learned, and Vespers has become a recited Office with a hymn at the end, which {@old_friar} calls, at recreation, the Presbyterian Vespers. The prior has asked whether anyone will take on the choir, which means teaching it, which means an hour a week with men who did not join to sing.

choices.label: Take the choir
choices.outcome: The hour is bad for a year and then not. The house sings Compline properly by the second Easter and the old friar weeps, once, in the stall, and says it was the smoke, and the priory's Sunday congregation, which had not known why it was thinner, is thicker.

choices.label: Get a student brother from the studium to teach it
choices.outcome: The student brother is a musician and an irritant, and the house learns to sing and to dislike him, and when he is professed and sent elsewhere the chant holds for a while and then does not, and it is your turn again.

choices.label: Say the recited Office is an Office too
choices.outcome: It is. The old friar does not speak to you for a week. The house recites for a decade, and the men who join in that decade join a house that recites, and do not know what they have not had.

events.title: The Diocesan Friend
events.body: {@brother_priest} was ordained the same June as you, for the diocese, and has been the friend you have had outside the order ever since: dinner once a month, the priory or his rectory, a bottle, and an honesty about both institutions that is possible only between men who belong to different ones. This month he has said he is thinking of asking to enter the order, since his diocese is not what he hoped, and has asked what you think.

choices.label: Tell him the truth: the order is not what he hopes either
choices.outcome: He is quiet and then laughs, and does not enter, and is a good pastor for thirty years, and says at your jubilee that you saved him from the friars, and it is the best toast anyone gives.

choices.label: Tell him what the order gave you and let him decide
choices.outcome: He enters. He is a novice at forty, in a house where the novices are twenty-four, and it is hard and he stays, and is a friar you are glad of, and the dinners stop, since you are brothers now and brothers do not need them, and you miss them.

choices.label: Send him to the provincial, since it is not yours to say
choices.outcome: The provincial sees him twice and says no, kindly, for reasons the provincial does not tell you, and the friend is hurt and thinks you knew, and the dinners are thinner for a year and then are not.

events.title: The Studium Wants You
events.body: The regent has written, through the provincial, since that is the road: the studium wants a lecturer in the thing you know, three years, a cell at the studium, and the student brothers in your hands for that long. It is the road to the regency, if you want the regency. {@prior} says the house will manage and says it in the voice of a man who is not sure it will.

choices.label: Go to the studium
choices.outcome: Three years and then six. You are a teacher, it turns out, of the kind the student brothers argue about at recreation, and the regency is a thing the province begins to say your name near, and the house you left has a different prior and a different smell when you visit.

choices.label: Stay; the house needs a preacher more than the studium needs a lecturer
choices.outcome: The regent is not pleased and the prior is. The studium takes a man from another province who is very good, and the road to the regency closes without a sound, and you preach, and the priory church is full.

choices.label: Offer a course a semester, commuting
choices.outcome: The regent takes it, since half of you is worth having. It is a long drive on Wednesdays for six years and the student brothers know you as the Wednesday man, and the house has you the other six days, mostly, and the regency goes to someone who was there all week.

events.title: Rome Wants a Year
events.body: The order's general curia has written to the provincial for a friar to spend a year at the house in Rome on a piece of work the order needs done, and the provincial, who was marked for it once himself and did not go, has named you. It is a year away from the house and the province, in a city where the order is old and the friars are from forty countries and the coffee is better than the theology, {@provincial} says, and the theology is good.

choices.label: Go to Rome
choices.outcome: Rome. The year is a life in a small compass: the order as it is everywhere, men from Kraków and Manila and Lagos at one table, and a view of your own province from far enough away to see it whole. You come back with a language and a friend on three continents and a reputation at the curia, which is a thing that outlasts provincials.

choices.label: Decline; the house is in the middle of something
choices.outcome: The provincial sends the next name. The house's middle of something ends, as they do, and it is a year before you know what you declined, which is when the other friar comes back with the language and the friends and the reputation.

choices.label: Ask him why he did not go
choices.outcome: He tells you, since you asked: a house that needed him, he thought, and did not, and a provincial who let him stay, and thirty years of wondering. He says to go. You go, and write to him from Rome, and he keeps the letters.

events.title: The Procurator's Books
events.body: The house's procurator has died, suddenly, in March, and the books are in the state a good man's books are in when nobody else has looked at them for nineteen years. The prior has asked you to take the office, since you are, he says, the only man in the house who can read a bank statement without moving his lips, and the alternative is a layman from the diocese, which the house would feel.

choices.label: Take the books
choices.outcome: You take them. It is a year of evenings and a house that does not know what it costs, and by the second year it does, and the prior says at chapter that the house is solvent for the first time in living memory, and the friars look at you as if you had done something faintly improper.

choices.label: Ask for the layman, and sit with him
choices.outcome: The layman is good and patient and the house does not feel it as much as it feared. You learn the books from him without holding them, and when he retires you take them, easily, since you know where everything is.

choices.label: Say you are a preacher and the books are the prior's problem
choices.outcome: The prior does the books himself for two years and does them badly and the province sends an auditor, and the house has a hard year of it, and the prior does not blame you, in words.

events.title: The Vocation Road
events.body: The province's vocation director has asked you to go with him on the spring road: nine colleges in eleven days, a talk in a chaplaincy lounge each night, a Mass in the morning, and the twenty-year-olds who come up afterward and ask, in one form or another, whether it is a real life. He says you are the friar they should see, since you look as if you have slept, which he has not.

choices.label: Go on the road
choices.outcome: Eleven days and four thousand miles. Three of the twenty-year-olds write to the province afterward and one enters, and is professed six years later with your name in the story he tells at profession, and the vocation director asks you every spring after, and you go, most springs.

choices.label: Go, and tell them it is a real life and a hard one
choices.outcome: The talks are the honest kind and the vocation director winces at two of them and does not correct you, and the boys who write afterward are fewer and stay longer, and one of them is a novice master forty years later and says it was the honesty.

choices.label: Say the house cannot spare you in Lent
choices.outcome: It cannot. He goes alone and comes back grey and is replaced the next year, and the man who replaces him asks you, and you go then, in a better season.

events.title: A Brother in the Paper
events.body: A friar of the province, not of your house, is in the morning paper, accused of a thing the paper says with care and the province will say with less, since it is true. The house is quiet at breakfast. The priory church has a Sunday and you are preaching it, and the people who come will have read the paper, and {@prior} has said only that you should preach the Gospel, which is what he says every week.

choices.label: Name it from the pulpit: what happened, what the province is doing, and what the people are owed
choices.outcome: The church is silent in the way churches are when someone has said the thing. Two families leave. Forty people stay after Mass to talk to the friars, which has never happened. The province's office hears the homily quoted and does not know, for a month, whether to be grateful, and is.

choices.label: Preach the Gospel, and say a sentence at the end
choices.outcome: The sentence is heard. It is enough for most and not for some, and the some write to the prior, and the prior, reading the letters, says you were right and that he would have said two sentences, and the church is a little emptier for a year.

choices.label: Say nothing; the province will speak
choices.outcome: The province speaks on Tuesday, in a statement. The church heard nothing on Sunday and remembers that it heard nothing, and the priory's Sunday congregation is thinner for two years, and the prior does not say whose homily it was.
